title: AI Personality Repeatability: Labels vs Answer Variance
description: Compare unique answer vectors, modal results and score variation across 2,000 assessments. Stable labels can conceal changing questionnaire answers.
h1: Does a stable result mean a stable AI personality?
dek: A model can get the exact same personality label 100 times in a row while changing dozens of individual answers underneath.
lede: Getting the same four-letter type across 100 runs doesn't mean the model gave the same answers every time. Using our 2,000 September 2026 test sessions, we separated three things: identical answer sheets, score variation, and repeated final labels.
answer: All 400 fresh Attachment runs scored Secure, yet the four models produced 90, 100, 79, and 96 different answer sheets out of 100. A steady label often hides shifting individual answers.

sections.html:
• Identical answer sheets (vector repetition): Did the model pick the exact same numbers on every single question?
  • Score stability: How much did the numeric totals move from run to run?
  • Label stability: How often did the final category (like INTJ or Secure) stay the same?

Because a broad category covers a wide range of scores, a model's final label can stay 100% constant even when its underlying answers change on almost every run.

Each cell shows how many unique answer sheets appeared across 100 fresh runs. Shorter tests like DISC (16 questions) naturally repeat exact answer sheets more often than longer tests like the Big Five (50 questions).

sections.h2: On DISC, Opus 5.5 gave the exact same 16 answers 60 times
sections.html:
Across 100 DISC runs, Claude Opus 5.5 produced only 7 distinct answer sheets—and its single most common answer sheet appeared 60 times. Claude Fable 5.1 produced 10 distinct DISC sheets (top sheet: 45 times), while GPT-6 Sol produced 66 distinct sheets (top sheet: 8 times).

Remember that Opus and Fable took one hidden-name test per session, while Astra and Sol took all five named tests inside one Codex session. Both prompt style and sampling settings affect how much answers vary.

sections.h2: 100% Secure labels, but up to 100 different answer sheets
sections.html:
Every single run across all four models (400/400) landed in the Secure Attachment quadrant. Yet GPT-6 Sol gave a different set of 36 answers on all 100 runs, Fable gave 96 unique sheets, Astra gave 90, and Opus gave 79. Any anxiety and avoidance averages below 4.00 get bucketed into Secure.

On MBTI, keeping tied axes open shows 98 resolved INTJ runs for Fable vs. 45 resolved ISTJ and 19 resolved INTJ runs for Astra (see our tie-breaking study).

sections.h2: Why averages need standard deviations beside them
sections.html: GPT-6 Sol’s Neuroticism score averaged 20.05 out of 50 with a standard deviation of 5.35 points from run to run. Its Agreeableness score averaged 44.99 with a standard deviation of just 1.01 points. Looking only at the average hides which traits bounce around between sessions.

sections.h2: How to test whether your AI is consistent on real work
sections.html: Survey repeatability doesn't prove a model will follow your instructions on real tasks. To test real consistency, run the same task prompt 5–10 times in fresh chats and check observable rules: Did it put the conclusion first? Did it challenge a flawed assumption? Did it stay under your word limit? Download the 20-row repeatability CSV to inspect all counts from this study.
